1-1The Origin of Life

Decision flow
  1. Simple inorganic molecules (H₂O, CH₄, NH₃, CO₂…) + energy → small organic molecules
  2. Small molecules condense into polymers (loss of H₂O); reverse = hydrolysis
  3. Polymers that act as templates for complementary copies → self-replication
  4. Replicators subject to natural selection → compartments (cells)

Life on Earth is at least ~3.5 billion years old (microfossils of filamentous bacteria). The early atmosphere and energy sources (lightning, UV, hydrothermal vents) could produce organic compounds.

1-1A Biological Molecules Arose from Inorganic Materials

Living matter is made mostly of C, H, O, N (plus P, S, Ca, K, Na, Cl, Mg…). The Miller–Urey experiment (1953) passed an electric discharge through H₂O, CH₄, NH₃ and H₂ and produced water-soluble organics including several amino acids.

Hydrothermal vents (“black smokers”) are an alternative setting for prebiotic chemistry: hot, mineral-rich water provides energy and catalytic metal sulfides.

Biomolecules are built from a limited set of functional groups and linkages (Table 1-2): amino, hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl, sulfhydryl, phosphoryl groups; ester, ether, amide, thioester, phosphoester, phosphoanhydride linkages.

A carboxylic acid + an amine → amide + H₂O: a condensation reaction; the reverse is hydrolysis. Macromolecules also interact noncovalently, e.g., an ⁺NH₃ group with a COO⁻ group (complementary association).

1-1B Complex Self-Replicating Systems Evolved from Simple Molecules

Major biological polymers: proteins ← amino acids; nucleic acids ← nucleotides; polysaccharides ← monosaccharides (Table 1-3).

A polymer whose units pair with complementary units can serve as a template: complementary monomers line up, are joined, and separate — producing a copy (Fig. 1-5). In nucleic acids this complementarity is base pairing.

Because copying is imperfect, variants arise; those that replicate better increase in number → natural selection at the molecular level. The RNA world hypothesis: early life used RNA both as genetic material and as catalyst.

Enclosing replicators in a membrane (compartmentation) kept the products of useful reactions close by — the origin of cells.

1-2A Cells Carry Out Metabolic Reactions

Advantages of compartmentation: protection from the environment, high local concentrations of components, faster reactions. Early metabolism needed catalysts (metal ions, then polymeric catalysts).

Simple compounds are converted to complex ones by metabolic pathways. Photosynthesis evolved to use the sun's energy; its O₂ by-product changed the atmosphere and allowed aerobic respiration.

1-2B There Are Two Types of Cells: Prokaryotes and Eukaryotes

Decision flow
  1. Is there a membrane-enclosed nucleus? → yes: eukaryote / no: prokaryote
  2. Prokaryote: typically 1–10 μm, single circular DNA in the nucleoid, cell wall
  3. Eukaryote: ~10–100 μm, organelles (mitochondria, ER, Golgi, lysosomes…), cytoskeleton

Prokaryotes lack a nucleus; their DNA sits in the nucleoid. Common shapes: rods (bacilli), spheres (cocci), spirals (spirilla). E. coli is the best-studied.

Eukaryotic cells contain a nucleus and membrane-bounded organelles: mitochondria (oxidative metabolism), endoplasmic reticulum (protein/lipid synthesis; rough ER has ribosomes), Golgi apparatus (processing/sorting), lysosomes, peroxisomes; plants also have chloroplasts and a cell wall. The cytoskeleton gives shape and movement.

1-2C Molecular Data Reveal Three Evolutionary Domains of Organisms

Comparing sequences (e.g., rRNA) divides life into three domains: Bacteria, Archaea (prokaryotes, often in extreme environments) and Eukarya. Archaea share many molecular features with eukaryotes.

Endosymbiosis (Margulis): mitochondria and chloroplasts descended from free-living bacteria engulfed by an ancestral cell — they still have their own DNA and ribosomes.

1-2D Organisms Continue to Evolve

Evolution continues through mutation and natural selection — e.g., bacteria rapidly evolve antibiotic resistance. Multicellular organisms arose through cell differentiation and specialization.

1-3Thermodynamics

Decision flow
  1. Energy conserved? → 1st law: ΔU = q − w; at constant P use enthalpy ΔH = qP
  2. Disorder? → 2nd law: spontaneous processes increase the entropy of the universe
  3. Combine at constant T, P → ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
  4. ΔG < 0 → spontaneous (exergonic); ΔG > 0 → nonspontaneous (endergonic); ΔG = 0 → equilibrium

Thermodynamics describes energy changes; it predicts whether a process can occur, not how fast. System + surroundings = universe.

1-3A The First Law of Thermodynamics States That Energy Is Conserved

ΔU = Ufinal − Uinitial = q − w (q = heat absorbed by the system, w = work done by the system). Energy is neither created nor destroyed. U is a state function (depends only on initial and final states).

Most biological processes occur at constant pressure → use enthalpy H = U + PV. At constant P, ΔH = qP (for liquids/solids ΔH ≈ ΔU). ΔH < 0 = exothermic; ΔH > 0 = endothermic. Units: joule (J); 1 cal = 4.184 J.

📄 Textbook page p.13 — text could not be extracted, shown as a page image

1-3B The Second Law of Thermodynamics States That Entropy Tends to Increase

Entropy is a measure of disorder: S = kB ln W (W = number of equivalent arrangements, kB = Boltzmann constant). Spontaneous processes increase the entropy of the universe (system + surroundings).

At constant T, ΔS ≥ q/T. Living organisms can decrease their own entropy (become highly ordered) only by increasing the entropy of their surroundings even more.

1-3C The Free Energy Change Determines the Spontaneity of a Process

Gibbs free energy: G = H − TS, so at constant T and P, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. ΔG < 0: exergonic, spontaneous; ΔG > 0: endergonic; ΔG = 0: at equilibrium.

ΔHΔSSpontaneity
−+always spontaneous
−−spontaneous only below T = ΔH/ΔS
++spontaneous only above T = ΔH/ΔS
+−never spontaneous

A spontaneous reaction is not necessarily fast; the rate depends on the activation energy (and on catalysts/enzymes).

1-3D Free Energy Changes Can Be Calculated from Reactant and Product Concentrations

For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln([C]c[D]d/[A]a[B]b). R = 8.3145 J·K⁻¹·mol⁻¹.

At equilibrium ΔG = 0, so ΔG°′ = −RT ln K′eq and K′eq = e−ΔG°′/RT. K′eq > 1 ⇔ ΔG°′ < 0.

Biochemical standard state (′): 25°C, 1 atm, all solutes 1 M except [H⁺] = 10⁻⁷ M (pH 7); [H₂O] is taken as 1 (its 55.5 M is included in the constant).

Le Châtelier's principle: a system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance by shifting to counteract it. ΔG values are additive: an endergonic reaction can be driven by coupling to a more exergonic one (e.g., ATP hydrolysis).

In cells, reactions near equilibrium (ΔG ≈ 0) are freely reversible; those far from equilibrium (large negative ΔG) are control points of metabolic pathways.

📄 Textbook page p.18 — text could not be extracted, shown as a page image

1-3E Life Achieves Homeostasis While Obeying the Laws of Thermodynamics

Living things are open systems: they exchange matter and energy with their surroundings and are never at equilibrium. They maintain a steady state (homeostasis) in which inflow and outflow balance.

Energy flow in the biosphere: sunlight → photosynthesis (CO₂ + H₂O → carbohydrates) → organisms oxidize carbohydrates → CO₂ + H₂O; energy is ultimately lost as heat.

KCKey concepts

  • Biological molecules are built from a limited set of elements, functional groups and linkages.
  • Chemical evolution: simple compounds → condensation into polymers → self-replicating molecules subject to natural selection.
  • Cells are prokaryotic (no nucleus) or eukaryotic (nucleus + organelles).
  • Three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya.
  • 1st law: energy is conserved; 2nd law: spontaneous processes increase the entropy of the universe.
  • ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; ΔG < 0 → spontaneous. ΔG°′ = −RT ln K′eq.
  • Living organisms are open systems that maintain a steady state, not equilibrium.

QSelf-check

Self-check questions (8)

Answer in your head first, then tap the blank.

  1. Name the reaction that joins monomers into polymers with loss of water, and its reverse.

    → Condensation; hydrolysis

  2. What property of nucleic acids allows them to act as templates?

    → Complementarity (base pairing)

  3. Which organelles are thought to descend from engulfed bacteria?

    → Mitochondria and chloroplasts

  4. A reaction has ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0. When is it spontaneous?

    → Only above T = ΔH/ΔS

  5. If K′eq = 1, what is ΔG°′?

    → 0

  6. What is special about the biochemical standard state?

    → [H⁺] = 10⁻⁷ M (pH 7) instead of 1 M; [H₂O] taken as 1

  7. Can an endergonic reaction occur in a cell? How?

    → Yes — by coupling to a more exergonic reaction (e.g., ATP hydrolysis)

  8. Why are living organisms not at equilibrium?

    → They are open systems with continuous matter/energy flow (steady state)
